Subject: Re: Acme discovery — performance SLOs (recap & next steps)

Thanks again for taking the call today, Jill — helpful discussion. Quick recap and agreed next steps so we have a single thread:

1) SLOs and targets you shared:
- p95 latency (first token): <= 300ms for text-generation streaming workload
- sustained throughput: ~50 req/s with typical payloads ~1.2k tokens/request
- concurrency: peak of 200 concurrent requests (spiky traffic from UI and background jobs)
- connection pooling: prefer persistent HTTP/2 connections from our app servers, ~100 pooled connections across 10 instances
- streaming: require low-latency first token + steady streaming tail, ability to cut downstream on end-of-stream quickly

2) Redwood asks/clarifications:
- Can you share typical request/response token histogram? (mean, p90, p99) — Jill said she would attach sample traffic this week.
- Do you expect long-lived open streams (for assistant-style chat) or short single-turn generation mostly?

3) Next steps:
- Jill: send token histogram + contact for procurement
- Redwood (Dev + me): propose concurrency/rate-limit plan and a draft quote for dedicated or committed capacity options
- Follow-up call: Wed/Thu next week to review formal quote and procurement path

I'll loop Dev for technical sizing; Ethan will own commercial/quote.

Best,
Marissa

Thanks Marissa, great summary. A few clarifications and additional details from our engineering team:

- Token distribution (approx): mean 1,200 tokens, p90 2,200, p99 ~4,800. Most requests are single-turn generation but we also have a small subset (~10%) of multi-turn assistant sessions that keep streams open for up to ~90s.
- Concurrency: yes, peak concurrent requests can reach ~200 across our fleet. The UI opens persistent connections from 10 app instances, each with ~10 pooling connections (so ~100 persistent connections in steady-state).
- Burst behavior: we can get brief bursts up to 400 concurrent requests for ~30-60s during releases or feature flag flips.
- Latency: target for interactive flows is p95 first-token <= 300ms. For background tasks we can accept higher tail latency but prefer cost-optimized paths.

Attaching the token histogram and a sample request log. Procurement contact is procurement@acme.com.

Thanks for the details — reviewed the histogram and sample logs. Notes from a technical sizing perspective:

1) Feasibility:
- Hosted (standard tier): can meet p95 first-token <=300ms for the described payloads under typical load, but sustained 200 concurrent requests with 400 short spikes will push into higher-cost autoscaling and potential short-lived throttling at default tenant rate limits.
- Dedicated (reserved capacity): recommended if Acme requires zero-throttle guarantees during spikes and predictable unit economics. A modest Dedicated pool sized for ~60-80k tokens/sec sustained (roughly correlates to the 50 req/s with 1.2k tokens avg + buffer) should give comfortable headroom for 200 concurrent steady-state and 400 burst.

2) Rate limits & recommended quota model:
- Default hosted account limits: 30 req/s per tenant + short bursts via token bucket up to ~3x for <60s.
- For this deal, proposal: increase to 200 concurrent request allowance + 120 req/s sustained (to cover bursts) on the account with rate-limit headers communicated to client. Implement connection-based pooling limits (we can honor 100 persistent connections).
- Burst policy: policy-based temporary burst: allow up to 400 concurrent for up to 60s before graceful throttling kicks in; require pre-scheduled release windows for guaranteed higher burst capacity.

3) Streaming:
- Our runtime supports low-latency first token for streaming. We'll reserve KV cache + batching knobs to minimize P95. We recommend enabling prefix caching for repeated prompts and using gRPC or HTTP/2 to keep stream overhead low.

4) Next steps for a formal quote:
- Commercial: provide a dedicated capacity quote vs hosted quota increase + burst add-on. Ethan — can you prepare the commercial side? Marissa — I'll attach a short technical appendix about concurrency behavior and rate-limit headers so Jill's team can plan connection pooling.

Attaching a draft quote to include in the next email.
